tomshardware: TSMC says it will stay a pure logic foundry, denying a report that Nvidia pushed it toward 3D DRAM.

There was a report that TSMC began drafting 3D DRAM plans after a request from Nvidia, its largest customer.

Nvidia has reason to look, because AI demand has drained DRAM supply and turned memory into the part that decides whether accelerators ship.

3D DRAM stacks memory cells vertically to raise capacity per wafer, yet even Micron plans at least 4 more planar nodes before adopting it.

That timeline means a TSMC entry couldn’t ease shortages for at least 5 years, and TSMC lacks a competitive planar DRAM process to build from.

Instead, it already profits from memory without making it, by building HBM base dies and bonding memory to logic with SoIC hybrid bonding.

Separately, a Korean report says Nvidia wants Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to build its custom NVHBM base dies on TSMC’s 3nm process, which would give TSMC memory revenue without DRAM’s price swings.

⚛️ THE QUANTUM FRONTIER #012

Why do quantum computers make so many mistakes? 🧠

Imagine building a powerful computer where even tiny disturbances can corrupt a calculation.

That's one of quantum computing's biggest challenges.

Quantum information is incredibly fragile.

🌡️ Temperature fluctuations
📡 Electromagnetic interference
⚡ Imperfect quantum operations

All can introduce errors.

So how do scientists solve this?

Through quantum error correction.

Instead of relying on one fragile physical qubit, researchers combine multiple physical qubits to protect one logical qubit.

Think of it as a team working together to protect a single piece of information.

🔹 Physical qubits = the hardware
🔹 Logical qubits = protected quantum information
🔹 Error correction = the protection system

But there's a catch.

Protecting quantum information requires additional hardware and sophisticated error detection.

That's why more qubits doesn't automatically mean a better quantum computer.

The real race is about making quantum calculations reliable enough to be useful.

And that brings us one step closer to fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Next: What exactly is a logical qubit?

QUANTUM explained in plain language , for once.
A quantum computer is not just a faster laptop. It is a different kind of machine, built to solve a small set of very hard problems that ordinary computers cannot solve in any reasonable time. The most urgent is security: the math that protects our bank accounts, our messages, and our military communications today could one day be broken by a powerful enough quantum computer. That day is not here yet, but new security standards are already in place.
first forget the magic machine. 
You have probably heard a quantum computer described as a magic machine that "tries every answer at once" or is simply a super-fast version of the computer you already own. Neither description is true.
Your laptop, your phone, and the servers that run the internet are classical computers. They store information as bits — tiny switches that are either off (0) or on (1). Everything they do, from playing a video to running a bank, comes down to flipping those switches in the right order.
A quantum computer does not just flip those switches faster. It uses the strange rules of atoms and subatomic particles to work in a different way altogether. That makes it useless for most everyday jobs, but enormously powerful for a few specific mathematical problems.
secondly The qubit: is a switch that can be in - between.
The basic building block of a quantum computer is called a qubit. A qubit is the quantum version of a bit — the smallest unit of information in the machine.
A normal bit is either 0 or 1. A qubit can be in a state called superposition. Superposition means the qubit holds a blend of 0 and 1 at the same time, until you measure it. Only when you measure it does it settle into a definite 0 or 1.
Think of a coin spinning in the air. While it spins, it is neither heads nor tails — it is a blur of both. Only when it lands do you get a definite answer. A qubit is like that spinning coin, except the blend can be carefully controlled and used in a calculation.
thrice Entanglement: is/are where/when qubits that act as one
When two or more qubits become entangled, they stop behaving like separate pieces. Entanglement is a link between qubits so strong that what happens to one instantly relates to what happens to the other, no matter how far apart they are.
Imagine two coins that always land on opposite sides, even if you flip them in different rooms. That is the flavour of entanglement: the qubits are no longer independent. They act as one connected system.
Because of this, a group of qubits can hold far more connected information than the same number of ordinary bits.
Now , Interference: thats cancelling the wrong answers
Here is the part most explanations get wrong. A quantum computer does not simply try every possible answer in parallel and pick the right one. If it did, measuring it would just give you a random answer.
Instead, quantum computers use interference. Interference is the same effect you see when waves meet in water: two waves can add together and get bigger, or cancel each other out and disappear.
A quantum calculation is set up so that the paths leading to wrong answers cancel each other out, while the path leading to the right answer gets stronger and stronger. By the time you measure the result, the correct answer is the one most likely to show up.
next point to make here is, Why these machines are so fragile
If the basic ideas have been understood since the 1990s, why is there no quantum computer in every office? Because qubits are extraordinarily fragile. The effect that makes them powerful — their delicate blended state — is easily destroyed by the outside world. This loss is called decoherence. Decoherence is what happens when heat, a stray magnetic field, a vibration, or even a cosmic ray bumps into a qubit and knocks it out of its careful blend.
To slow that down, the most common kind of quantum computer, built by companies like IBM and Google, keeps its qubits in special refrigerators cooled to about 15 millikelvin — fifteen thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, colder than deep space.
Even then, errors are common. A classical computer makes a mistake less than once in a quadrillion operations. A current quantum computer makes a mistake roughly once in every hundred to a thousand operations. That is why today's machines are called NISQ machines — short for "noisy intermediate-scale quantum" — noisy, and with only tens to hundreds of qubits, not the thousands of reliable ones needed for the biggest jobs.
6th point Error correction: many qubits to make one good one
The fix is called quantum error correction. Error correction is a way of spreading one piece of information across many physical qubits, so that if a few of them go wrong, the information itself survives — like writing an important message in several copies and comparing them.
In a quantum computer, many imperfect physical qubits are combined to make one protected logical qubit — a single reliable unit of information. The leading method is called a surface code, which arranges qubits in a flat grid and checks them for errors without reading the information itself. Another approach, called quantum LDPC codes, tries to do the same job with fewer physical qubits per logical qubit.
The catch is the overhead: you may need hundreds or even thousands of physical qubits to make one good logical qubit. That is the main reason a truly reliable, large-scale quantum computer is still years away.
The real problem today: your security
The most immediate impact of quantum computing is not faster drug discovery or better financial models. It is data security.
Almost everything you do online is protected by a kind of encryption called asymmetric public-key cryptography. That is a system where you have a public key everyone can see, and a private key only you hold. The two best-known versions are called RSA and ECC. RSA is named after its inventors and is used widely for secure web traffic and banking. ECC, short for elliptic curve cryptography, does the same job with shorter keys and is used in phones, messaging apps, and secure connections.
RSA and ECC work because they rest on mathematical problems that are extremely hard for ordinary computers: splitting a very large number into its prime factors, and a related problem involving curves.
In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor showed that a large enough, reliable quantum computer could solve those same problems quickly. Shor's algorithm is a quantum recipe for factoring large numbers. Run on a machine with several thousand stable logical qubits, it would make today's RSA and ECC encryption effectively useless.
That machine does not exist yet. But the threat is already real, because of a practice called "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later." That means an adversary intercepts and stores encrypted messages today — diplomatic cables, business secrets, military communications — and simply waits. Years from now, when a powerful quantum computer exists, they decrypt the stored messages. Anything that needs to stay secret for a long time is at risk right now.
The new standards: what replaces RSA?
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, known as NIST, has spent years running a global competition to find replacement encryption that even a quantum computer cannot easily break. These replacements are called post-quantum cryptography — encryption designed to resist both ordinary computers and quantum computers.
In August 2024, NIST finalised the first three standards:
ML-KEM, standard FIPS 203. ML-KEM is the new standard for general encryption — locking up a message so only the intended reader can open it. It was previously known as CRYSTALS-Kyber, and it is based on a type of hard maths involving high-dimensional grids, called lattice-based cryptography.
ML-DSA, standard FIPS 204. ML-DSA is the new standard for digital signatures — the electronic seals that prove a message or a piece of software really came from who it claims to come from. It was previously known as CRYSTALS-Dilithium, and it is also lattice-based.
SLH-DSA, standard FIPS 205. SLH-DSA is a backup signature standard based on hash functions — the one-way scrambling functions used to check that data has not been tampered with. It was previously known as SPHINCS+. SLH-DSA is stateless hash-based, which means it does not need to keep track of which signatures it has already used.
All three were finalised on 13 August 2024. They are the foundation of the move away from RSA and ECC, and organisations are already starting to adopt them.
9. What to do about it: a practical roadmap
You do not need a physics degree to prepare:
First, take stock. Make a list of everywhere your organisation uses RSA or ECC — website certificates, VPN tunnels, email, and long-term data archives. You cannot replace what you have not found.
Second, use hybrid key exchange. Hybrid key exchange means using both the old and the new encryption at the same time, so that if one fails, the other still protects you. Modern protocols such as TLS 1.3 (the security behind the padlock in your browser) and OpenSSH (used to log into servers securely) are already adding this. Pair a classical method with ML-KEM, and you get protection against both today's attackers and tomorrow's quantum ones.
Third, try it yourself. You can experiment with real quantum hardware and simulators today, for free, using open-source Python toolkits. Qiskit, built by IBM, is the most widely used toolkit for designing quantum circuits and testing algorithms. Cirq, built by Google, is focused on today's noisy machines. Both let you write a few lines of code and see a quantum calculation run — no refrigerator required.
10. The bottom line
Quantum computing is moving from theory to engineering. The machines are still fragile, cold, and error-prone, and a fully reliable commercial quantum computer is still years away. But the security change is happening now.
The lesson is simple: quantum computers will not make your laptop faster, and they will not replace ordinary computers. What they will do is change the maths underneath our security. The organisations that take stock, adopt the new NIST standards, and use hybrid encryption now will be ready. The ones that wait will find that the messages they sent years ago are no longer secret.
Understanding qubits, error correction, and post-quantum security is not about science fiction. It is about telling hype from the real change already under way.

Well damn. It's Monday, and apparently the internet has finally perfected an AI model with 100% accuracy. It's called Kick a Man While He's Down, trained on 40 trillion tokens of outrage, moral superiority and people who've never built a damn thing explaining how everyone else should live.

And today's exhibit is NVIDIA's Jensen Huang.

Look, Jensen screwed up. He admitted it, apologized to his family and colleagues, and accepted responsibility. NVIDIA's board is doing their due diligence and investigating separate national-security concerns, which absolutely deserve serious scrutiny. No one gets a free pass because they invented a GPU architecture worth several trillion dollars.

But something about our culture has become genuinely disturbing. We used to celebrate success together, criticize failures constructively, and occasionally help someone get back on their feet. Now the social contract treats another person's downfall like entertainment with 80,000 anonymous accounts examining a wardrobe malfunction.

The algorithms reward the pile-on, the spectators collect their moral superiority points, and nobody seems particularly interested in whether anything actually gets better, just goading more into their convenient outage. There's an enormous difference between demanding accountability and rooting for destruction. One builds a better world. The other just tries to buy friends, followers, impressions.

A strange way to reward a civilization.

The business and national-security story here  deserves attention. NVIDIA's board is acting responsibly. Huang says he'll cooperate.  An investigation is not a finding of guilt.  An allegation of espionage is not proof of a successful intelligence operation. 

NVIDIA earnings are next Tuesday, November 17.  So here's an uncomfortable business question. If NVIDIA has huge demand visibility, could the company withstand a leadership transition?

Conceptually, yes. A company with this much infrastructure momentum should have succession plans, an extraordinary management team, and operational systems that don't depend on a single individual. 

But nobody can seriously claim the NVIDIA ecosystem was built without Jensen's vision and execution.  Besides, the real question from an investor's perspective isn't whether the next 12 months look promising. It's whether NVIDIA can keep delivering through 2028 and beyond, when customers have more alternatives.

Now, onto the models, because the labs apparently decided to spend another weekend playing hide-and-seek. Qwen 4 is rumbling around, but not here yet. GPT-6.2 Sol has lots of chatter.  A creator claims Codex sessions using GPT-6.1 Sol may already be silently routed to a newer checkpoint. Speculation, not proof.

Quantum computers make errors. Lots of them, three 9s can be a great run. To perform dependable calculations, quantum systems need to repeatedly measure error syndromes and determine how to correct the underlying information. That decoding work is classical computing, and it needs to happen quickly enough to keep pace with the quantum processor. 

The Department of Energy's 2028 target is 100 logical qubits performing 100,000 difficult operations. IBM cites experiments reaching 70 logical qubits and 438 such operations. That's approximately a 228X increase in operation count still to accomplish, along with increasing the logical-qubit count. IBM and AMD are attacking the engineering bottleneck, not merely adding more qubits to a press release.

You want more ? IBM unveiled a Quantum System Two in Chicago on Friday. Real equipment, real infrastructure, and researchers getting access to actual hardware. 

NVIDIA dominates the modern AI training and inference ecosystem, but quantum computing may create additional demand for high-performance classical accelerators. IBM and AMD are positioning themselves inside that emerging architecture. Whether it becomes a meaningful commercial market is still an open question, but the research is moving beyond isolated laboratory demonstrations.

Forward! Tomorrow, November 10, is busy! Anthropic has its Work at the Frontier briefing, will they bring gifts??? 

I remain extraordinarily optimistic about what AI and accelerated computing can accomplish. But I also think we ought to remember that the people building this future are human, capable of remarkable achievements and serious mistakes. Accountability matters. So does learning, and maybe updating our priors.

I'd encourage you to give the facts enough time to catch up with the outrage. Let's see what the week brings.

I'm still hopeful. 

Enjoy! Out.

so for anyone writing quantum code today the useful question is unglamorous. what does your abstraction layer look like when qubit count and error correction both move under you?

what would you want the platform to guarantee across generations: the same gate set or the same error model?

韩联社11月8日报道，受长期低出生率影响，韩国2027年小学一年级新生人数预计首次跌破30万，创有统计记录以来的最低水平。

根据韩国国家统计门户和韩国教育开发院的数据，2026年韩国小学新生共有301,442人，已经是1964年开始统计以来的最低纪录。2024年，新生人数才首次跌破40万，仅仅三年之后，就可能进一步降至30万以下。

新生人数急剧下降，主要与2020年出生人口大幅减少有关。当年韩国只有272,337名新生儿，比2019年减少10%。虽然实际入学人数还受到提前入学、海外居留和外国儿童等因素影响，但近年来入学人数与相应出生年份的人口规模相差不大。

韩国小学新生人数曾在1968年达到105.56万人的历史高峰。如果2027年降至20多万人，规模将仅相当于当年的四分之一左右。

人口减少正在改变韩国教育系统。韩国教育开发院今年8月公布的统计显示，全国小学生总数已经降至约221.94万人，比2025年减少约12.61万人，降幅为5.4%。

韩联社指出，首尔首都圈以外的学校可能面临更严重的生源不足问题。学校规模不断缩小，不仅可能加速学校合并或关闭，还会减少学生参与集体活动和多样化课程的机会，并可能促使更多有学龄儿童的家庭迁往首都圈。

未来几年，韩国小学新生人数预计继续下降，到2030年可能接近20万人。

虽然韩国出生人口已经从2024年开始回升，2025年增至254,341人，但出生人口回升对小学招生的影响仍需数年才能显现。

Approach — The long-term electrical stability, flexibility, & biocompatibility of the SWCNT arrays were investigated in vivo in laboratory rats by two-months recording & analysis of subdural electrocorticogram (ECoG). Main Results — The single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) arrays were able to capture high quality & very stable electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals across 8 weeks. I respect Jukan, but I feel a little frustrated whenever I see this kind of argument.

You can build any scenario around plausible assumptions, and yes, of course, the outcome will follow from those assumptions. If you assume demand collapses, customers accumulate inventory, and contract terms get renegotiated, then naturally, memory companies’ revenue and profits will decline.

But honestly, this feels like the perspective of analysts who treat memory as just a commodity you manufacture and sell, without properly understanding the technological changes taking place in custom memory.

Who exactly are these customers we are talking about when we say they could cancel LTAs or defer deliveries? They are the very customers working with memory companies to design the next generation of HBM and 3D stacked DRAM.

After jointly designing and validating these products, can customers really cancel those volumes so easily or push deliveries out by one or two years? How would they manufacture their own products, which were designed around that memory? What happens to the launch and system deployment schedules they have already coordinated? Switching suppliers also raises questions of design compatibility and requalification. If you are going to argue that contracts can be adjusted, you also need to explain what that decision would mean for the very customers canceling them.

This is one of the biggest reasons I keep saying that memory is no longer the same cyclical industry it used to be. The parties to these LTAs are already tied together from the design stage. But if you still view memory simply as a commodity where rising prices lead to more production, and inventory buildups lead to price cuts or canceled orders, you will inevitably miss this shift in the technical and business relationships.

One more thing. These arguments about a collapse in memory demand seem to assume that planned AI data center investments will be canceled on a massive scale, or that AI infrastructure expansion will slow so substantially that memory demand falls sharply. What interests me more than whether contracts can be adjusted is why you expect demand to weaken that dramatically in the first place.

I think it would be more realistic to discuss directly whether the AI era we expect will actually fail to materialize, and whether much of the AI infrastructure investment currently planned will disappear. If that is your outlook, I can at least understand why you would expect memory demand to collapse and customers to cut volumes even for products they have jointly developed.

What is Traumatic Brain Injury? ​

​Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a physical injury to the brain resulting from a variety of causes including vehicle crashes, falls, sports related injuries, military combat, and assaults. 

As a result, the severity of the injury can fluctuate in degree from mild to severe, sometimes resulting in death. 

While TBI mostly prompts physical damage to the brain, it is also associated with an array of psychological and hrmonal problems. 

These include cognitive disabilities, sleep pattern problems, lack of attention, dizziness, confusion, etc. 

Current Diagnosis of TBI

TBI is currently diagnosed with a subjective physical examination, psychological screen & the typical Glascow test. The patient's injury is usually confirmed with a CT scan. 

CT scans are effective in depicting bleeding around the brain as well as swelling, but limited in their ability to diagnose mild TBI, especially concussions. 

MRIs are more powerful in their imaging ability in comparison to CT scans. But like CT scans, they are unable to detect injury to nerve fibers inside the brain. 

Hence, axonal damage remains undetectable in most occasions. Other radiological exams like positron emission tomography scans are developed for mild TBI but with extremely high cost. 

The most successful first response test is the imPACT test, which is computerized version of the physical and psychological tests. It allows health care personnel to diagnose TBI at the scene of injury by using an integrated electronic applications, but not reliable.
